audience: People who have heard of Tau Net or hold AGRS and want to see what the testnet really does; then anyone curious about a blockchain with rules in logic.
question: How do I run my own Tau Net testnet node?
title: Run your own Tau Net testnet node: what it takes

scenes.say: Anyone can run a node on the Tau Net testnet. Yours then checks every block itself, instead of trusting ours. This is what it takes.
scenes.caption: Nodes online now

scenes.say: The quickest way is the Docker image from IDNI, the team that builds Tau Net. It builds the Tau engine inside. This page gives you the command to copy.
scenes.caption: One command

scenes.say: Be ready for an alpha. Nodes lose their peers, chains restart. Ours stood alone for two hours once, because it did not reconnect by itself. When that happens, we say so.
scenes.caption: Our own incidents

scenes.say: Once it runs, your node follows the chain block by block, like the one you are watching through now.
scenes.caption: Following the chain

scenes.say: And it refuses what breaks the rules, on its own. Every node does. That is why nobody has to be trusted to enforce them.
scenes.caption: Every node checks

scenes.say: If it fails to sync or loses peers, the logs are what helps most: IDNI asks for them as GitHub issues. Next: what the testnet is, from the start.
scenes.caption: Report what fails

description: What it takes to run a read node on the Tau Net testnet with IDNI's Docker image, what to expect from an alpha, and how to help by reporting what fails.

facts.run-node: the quickest way to run a node is IDNI's standalone Docker image, which builds the Tau engine inside it; anyone can run a read node (tauhud.com/facts/, fact 'run-node')
facts.own-incident: 14 November: our node stayed on the old chain for 2 hours after a testnet restart until it was restarted (tauhud.com/status/)
